summary: A 1977 note describing a time server, a service that provides the current time to other hosts on the network. Its status is unknown.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 738 specifies a brief exchange in which a client connects to a time server and receives a 32-bit value. The value counts seconds from midnight GMT on 1 January 1900.

subtitle: A simple network service that returns a host's current time as a binary value.

tldr.problem: Some hosts lacked a date and time clock, and human or machine errors could make their clocks wrong.
tldr.mechanism: A client connects to socket 37 without using ICP; the server sends a 32-bit time value and closes the connection.
tldr.outcome: The RFC describes an implemented method for hosts to poll independent sites and compare or correct their time.

today: RFC 738 describes the Time Server protocol as it was implemented on ITS hosts. The memo specifies its socket and time representation.

sections.title: Why a Time Server Was Proposed
sections.content:
The RFC says not all systems have a date and time clock and that clocks can be wrong because of human or machine error. A host can poll several independent time servers to confirm or correct its idea of the time.

The memo describes the protocol as implemented on ITS hosts.
sections.plainLanguage: A host without a reliable clock can ask other hosts for the time. Comparing answers from several independent sites can help confirm its clock.

sections.title: Connecting to the Server
sections.content:
The server listens on socket 37, written as 45 octal. The user connects to that socket without the usual Initial Connection Protocol, receives the time as a 32-bit binary number, and closes the connection; the server also closes it.

If the server cannot determine its time, it should refuse the connection or close without sending data.
sections.plainLanguage: The client connects directly to the time socket and reads one value. The server then closes the connection, or closes without data if it cannot determine the time.

sections.title: Representing the Time
sections.content:
The value is the number of seconds since midnight on 1 January 1900 GMT. The RFC says this base serves until the year 2036.

The memo gives the beginning of 1 January 1976 GMT as an example value of 2,398,291,200.
sections.plainLanguage: The returned number counts seconds from a fixed starting point: midnight GMT on 1 January 1900. The RFC states that the 32-bit value serves until 2036.
